Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:29: And on the verse King David, peace be upon him, said in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 29:15), "for we are strangers before You, and sojourners, as were all our fathers; our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no abiding," they said in Bereshit Rabbah (96:2 [sic]): "our days are as a shadow" - would that it were like the shadow of a wall or the shadow of a tree; rather, like the shadow of a bird, as it is said, "our days on the earth are as a shadow." "And there is no abiding [mikveh]" - there is none who hopes that he will not die; all know and say with their mouths that they will die - Abraham said (Genesis 15:2), "and I go childless"; Isaac said (ibid. 27:4), "that my soul may bless you before I die"; Jacob said (ibid. 47:30), "and I will lie with my fathers" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:30: And in Tanchuma (Parashat Vayelech), on the verse (Deuteronomy 31:14), "behold, your days approach that you must die," he said, in these words: this is what Scripture says (Proverbs 11:31), "behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth," and so on - of whom was this verse said? It was said only of Moses the righteous, than whom there was none like him among all the prophets, nor among all the wise men - for the Holy One, blessed be He, testified of him after his death (Deuteronomy 34:10), "and there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses." And yet, nevertheless, it was not in his power to save himself from death - how much more so other people! And so David said (1 Chronicles 29:15), "for we are strangers before You," and so on, "our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no abiding" - but was it not already said, "wait for the LORD"? The text teaches, "there is no abiding" - David said, for all a person's other conditions there is hope: the poor man, until he becomes rich; the weak man, until he becomes mighty; the sick man, until he is healed; the imprisoned man, who was in a prison house, until he is released. But for the day of death there is no hope - for the Holy One, blessed be He, spoke with Moses face to face, and he could not save himself from death. And so King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 9:2), "all things come alike to all," and so on - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:31: Therefore a person must repent while the soul is still given within his body, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (ibid. 9:10), "whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might" - and they said, of blessed memory, in the Midrash (Yalkut Kohelet, remez 989): repent while you have your strength; while the lamp still burns, give it oil before it is extinguished - once the lamp is out, oil no longer helps it at all - to this point. And behold, it is explained that the oil for the lamp is Torah and commandments, along the lines of (ibid. 9:8), "and let your head lack no oil," as I explained in the Gate of Love (chapter 4) - and along these lines they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Balak, page 187a) - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:32: And further they said in the Midrash (cf. Midrash Tehillim), on the verse "hear, O LORD, my righteousness" (Psalms 17:1): the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, while the gates of repentance are open, repent - for I accept bribes in this world, but once I sit in judgment for the World to Come, I do not accept bribes, as it is said (Proverbs 6:35), "he will not regard any ransom" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:33: And along these lines our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 6:6), "go to the ant, you sluggard": Rabbi Yehuda said, the wicked are destined to say before the Holy One, blessed be He, leave us and we will repent - and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers them: fools of the world, this world is like the eve of Shabbat, and the World to Come is like Shabbat - if a person does not prepare on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat? And likewise it is like the sea and the dry land - if he does not take from the dry land, he has nothing to eat at sea. And likewise it is like the summer days and the rainy days - if he does not plow, sow, and reap in the summer days, what will he eat in the rainy days? He should further have learned from the ant, as it is said, "go to the ant, you sluggard."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:34: Another interpretation: this ant has neither officer nor ruler, but does everything through its own wisdom - and you did not learn from it, out of your laziness and foolishness, and did not repent - therefore Solomon said (Proverbs 6:9), "how long will you sleep, O sluggard?" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:35: And I found in another version: after the three mentioned concerning this world and the World to Come, he further said: the world you were in is like a hallway, and the World to Come is like a banquet hall - prepare yourself in the hallway so that you may enter the banquet hall.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:36: And in Eleh HaDevarim Rabbah (5:2), also brought there in the Yalkut (Proverbs, section 938, page 134b), in explanation of the verse, it says that the ant lives only six months, and its entire food is a grain and a half; and it says, there was an incident, and they found the ant's storehouse to contain three hundred kor - therefore Solomon said, prepare for yourself commandments in this world for the World to Come. What is "consider her ways, and be wise"? The [good] conduct within her, that she flees from theft - Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta said, there was an incident with an ant that dropped a grain of wheat, and all the others came and smelled it, but none of them took it; the one to whom it belonged came and took it - and yet she has neither judge nor officer, as it is said, "which having no chief, overseer, or ruler" - you, who have appointed for yourselves officers, all the more so [should behave properly] - woe to the judges and officers! Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, this man is wretched, who must learn from the ant - had he learned and acted, he would not be wretched, but he must learn from her ways and has not learned - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:37: And it is fitting that one hasten greatly in the deed of service, and concerning this it is said (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 15), "the day is short and the work is great," and so they said in the Gemara (Ketubot 67b), "the provisions are light and the road is long" - for one traveling a year's journey must prepare provisions for a month or two months; for one traveling many years after his death, how much more so must he prepare!
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:38: And further they said (cf. Shabbat 30a) on the verse (Psalms 88:6), "free among the dead": Rabbi Yochanan said, once a person dies, he becomes free of the commandments - and this is what David says (ibid. 115:17), "the dead do not praise the LORD" - a person should occupy himself with Torah and commandments always before he dies, for once he dies he is idle from the commandments and from the Torah, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has no praise from him - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:39: And the acceptable repentance is in the time of one's youth, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "and remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah on this verse): we learn, Akavya ben Mahalalel says, contemplate three things and you will not come to sin: know from where you came, and to where you are going, and so on. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Levi: all three expounded from one word, "borecha" [your Creator] - "be'erecha" [your well, i.e., putrid fluid], "borecha" [your pit, i.e., worm and maggot], "borecha" [your Creator] - this is the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:40: "In the days of your youth" - Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar taught: while you find [strength] and it is available to you. "Before the evil days come" - these are the days of old age. "And the years arrive of which you shall say, I have no delight in them" - these are the days of the Messiah, in which there is neither merit nor liability [i.e., no more free-will testing]. "Before the sun grows dark" - this is the forehead, and so on - to this point, relevant here. And in Vayikra Rabbah (parashah 18) this discourse is cited, and there it says: "in the days of your youth" - in the days of your childhood, while your strength is upon you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:41: And further they said in Tractate Avodah Zarah, first chapter (19b), on the verse (Psalms 112:1), "happy is the man [ish] who fears the LORD" - in these words: "happy is the man," and not "happy is the woman" [ishah] - Rav Amram said in the name of Rav: happy is he who repents while he is [still vigorous as] a man. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: happy is he who overcomes his inclination like a man - to this point. And Rashi explained "when he is a man" as when he is young in his strength - meaning, he hastens to recognize his Creator before the days of old age, like a mighty man - to this point. And the difference between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rav is that, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, even an old man who repents and overcomes his inclination like a young man - happy is he; but for Rav, specifically when he is young [does the praise apply].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:42: And so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim, page 87b) on the verse "you shall rise before the aged" (Leviticus 19:32), in these words: we have further learned, this verse comes for exposition - "you shall rise before the aged," as the colleagues have aroused concerning it - it is a warning to a person, before he becomes old, that he rise to a good standing in the world, for it is fitting that he requite it at the end of his days - for there is no praise for a person when he is old and cannot be bad, but his praise is when he is in his strength and is good. And King Solomon cried out and said (Proverbs 20:11), "even a child is known by his deeds," and so on - along these lines it is written (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "and remember your Creator in the days of your youth," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:43: And along these lines they said in the Midrash (Zuta Kohelet, chapter 12), "for childhood and youth [sechorut] are vanity" (Ecclesiastes 11:10) - Rabbi Yitzchak said, things a person does in his youth blacken [mashchirim] his face in his old age - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:44: And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 227b) they wrote another reason concerning returning in repentance in the days of youth. He said there that a nut has a thin shell, such that when the nut is moist, it separates easily from the kernel - and this alludes to the evil inclination. They said, of blessed memory: and this shell is like the shell that clings to the kernel of a nut - and when the nut is soft, that shell separates from the kernel of the nut without difficulty, but when the nut is dry, it is hard for a person to remove it from there, for the hardness still stands in its place - and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded a person to return in repentance in his youth, before the evil inclination grows old within him - this is what is written, "you shall rise before the aged" - before your own old age - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:45: And this is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 29:21), "he who pampers his servant from childhood shall have him become a master [manon] in the end." And this servant is the evil inclination, who is a slave of slaves - and if in one's youth he pampers it with the pleasures of the world, "in the end it shall be manon" - a ruler over him, and it will be hard for him to subdue it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:46: A fifth awakening to repentance is the matter of the herald who proclaims above every day concerning repentance - and this is explained in several places in the Zohar, especially in Parashat Lech Lecha (page 77a), where he says there that at midnight, when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes into the lower Garden of Eden, a herald cries out with force and says: to you, supernal holy ones, speak - who among you enters wind into his ears, and so on. Woe to those who sleep the sleep of their holes, who do not know and do not consider where they will stand in the judgment of the reckoning appointed for when the body is defiled and the soul errs over the face of the midday air, ascending and descending, and the gates are not opened, and they roll among stones inside a sling - woe to them, who will seek them, that they not stand in this delight, in the places of the pleasures of the righteous, whose places are appointed - they are handed into the hand of Dumah, they descend and do not ascend; of them it is written (Job 7:9), "as the cloud is consumed and vanishes away, so he who goes down to Sheol shall come up no more" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:47: Further, in Parashat Vayetze (page 161b, in Sitrei Torah), in these words: the voice of a voice that cries out, aroused from above to below - we have our eyes open; a wheel turns from above in several directions, a pleasant voice - awaken, you sleepers, who sleep in your holes, and do not know, and do not consider, and do not see, your ears stopped, your hearts heavy, sleeping and not knowing; the Torah stands before you and you do not pay attention, and do not know what you gaze upon - you see and do not see; the Torah raises its voice: consider, you fools, open your eyes and know - there is none who pays attention and none who inclines his ear. How long will you remain in the darkness of your will? Look, to know, and the light that shone at the time complete Jacob, from the distress of the land and the other domain amid the strange ranks, pushed all of them away and chose the portion of his lot and his inheritance - light from within darkness, wisdom from within foolishness - and he honored his Master when he stood under the domain of another god - shall be revealed to you. Concerning this (Isaiah 29:22), "Jacob shall not now be ashamed, nor shall his face now grow pale" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:48: Further, in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 203b), in these words: come and see, every single day, when the light rises, a certain bird is aroused on the tree of the Garden of Eden, and calls three times, and a branch rises up, and a herald cries out with force: to you, gracious ones, I speak - who among you sees and does not see, who stand in the world and do not know for what they stand, and do not pay attention to the glory of their Master; the Torah stands before them and they do not labor in it - it would be better for them not to have been created; for what do they stand without understanding? Woe to them, when their evil days awaken upon them, and they are cast out of the world - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:49: And in Parashat Terumah (page 130b), Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained the daily proclamation of repentance, in these words: it is written (Isaiah 21:12), "the morning comes, and also the night; if you will inquire, inquire; return, come." This verse they established concerning the exile of Israel, who dwell among the children of Seir, and Israel say to the Holy One, blessed be He, "watchman, what of the night" - what shall become of us from the exile, which resembles the darkness of night? What is written? He says, "watchman" - this is the Holy One, blessed be He; "the morning comes" - light has already shone for all, and I raised you to My service, so that you merit the life of the world [eternal] - you abandoned My Torah; "and also the night" - I have brought you into exile as before. "If you will inquire, inquire" - along the lines of (ibid. 34:16), "seek from the book of the LORD, and read," and there you will find on what your exile depends, and your redemption - and when you inquire of it, it will say and proclaim before you, "return, come" - return in complete repentance, and immediately, "come," and be brought near to Me - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:50: And further on he gives another explanation of "he says, watchman, comes," and so on, in these words: "he says, watchman" - this is Metatron. "The morning comes" - this is the Shacharit prayer, which is the dominion of the day, that which rules over the night. And should you say that it comes alone, and male is separated from female - behold it is written, "and also the night" - both together, and they are never separated from one another; and this voice cries out with these words, "the morning comes, and also the night" - both are ready for you. From here on, "if you will inquire, inquire" - if you inquire your inquiries and return to your Master, "come" - as one who is ready to receive his children and have mercy on them; so too the Holy One, blessed be He, morning and also night, cries out and says, "come." Happy is the holy people, whose Master seeks them and calls them to bring them near to Him - then the holy people seek to gather in the synagogue, and whoever comes first is joined to the Shechinah in a single joining - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:51: Behold, it is explicit that Metatron the watchman proclaims repentance at the time of the Shacharit prayer and says, "the morning comes," and so on, "return, come." And likewise the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, called the dominion of the day and the dominion of the night, referred to in the verse as "morning" and "night," proclaim and say, "return, come." And this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, says in his words, "so too the Holy One, blessed be He, morning and also night, cried out and said, return, come." And according to this, the two proclamations mentioned in the verse are one from Metatron and one from the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah - and both, in truth, are one proclamation, for Metatron proclaims and says that the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, morning and also night, call their children and say, "return, come" - and the words of Rashbi, saying "so too the Holy One, blessed be He, morning," and so on, thus he explains the verse: "so too" - meaning, the proclamation of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, is also mentioned in the verse, that morning and night they call and say, "come."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:52: And further we learn from the general discourse that the essence of the prayer we pray is to appease our Owner, that He forgive our iniquities and that we return in complete repentance before Him - and this is what he says, "if you will inquire, inquire" - if you seek your requests before the holy King, "inquire" - pray and return to your Master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:53: And further we learn from the verse, in his saying "if you will inquire, inquire; return, come" - if you wish to ask requests of the Holy One, blessed be He, to pray, return in repentance first and afterward pray - for one who prays without repentance, of him it is said (Isaiah 1:12), "who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts?" And by this the wording of the verse is precise, in saying "if you will inquire" - for it should have said, "inquire; return, come" - why "if you will inquire"? The intent is as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:54: And further we learn from the discourse that one should not draw near to his Owner except after returning from his iniquities and casting away from himself all his transgressions - and this is what it says, "return, come," and Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in his words, "return in complete repentance, and immediately come and be brought near to Me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:55: And from the end of the discourse we further learn of His mercy, blessed be He, toward Israel, His treasured people, that He says to them "come," like one who is ready to receive his children and have mercy on them - and it is like the parable of a father who says to a son who has grown distant from him, "come to me, for I am ready and prepared to receive you." And who is there who would hear these words and not have his uncircumcised heart humbled, to return to his Father in Heaven? Since his Father is merciful and desires that the son draw near to Him, it is fitting that he not distance himself, Heaven forfend, nor stiffen his neck, but rise with alacrity from his sleep to come and entreat before the Shechinah in the synagogue with tears and prayer, so that they receive him - since the Shacharit prayer is a time of favor, as explained above in this regard, in the Gate of Love, chapter 11 - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:56: Further, concerning the matter of Metatron's proclamation, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained further on, on the verse (Isaiah 50:10), "who listens to the voice of His servant" - he said there, concerning one who comes early to the synagogue, that if one day he does not come, the Holy One, blessed be He, asks after him and says, "who among you fears the LORD, who listens to the voice of His servant" - in these words: and we have already aroused this concerning what is written (ibid. 21:11), "he calls to me out of Seir" - for it is level after level within level; that watchman cries out with force every single day, and this is "who listens to the voice of His servant" - this is Metatron - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:57: A sixth awakening to repentance: when a person reads the books of the Prophets, he will find that all of them proclaim concerning repentance. Hosea proclaims (14:2), "return, O Israel." Isaiah says (21:12), "if you will inquire, inquire; return, come; wash, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your doings from before My eyes," and so on (1:16). Jeremiah says (3:22), "return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings" - and many similar verses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:58: Ezekiel elaborated and explained the matters of repentance more than all the prophets. He said (Ezekiel 18:21), "but if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all My statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. All his transgressions that he has committed shall not be mentioned to him," and so on. "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? says the Lord GOD; and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" (ibid. 18:23). "Cast away from you all your transgressions, in which you have transgressed, and make you a new heart and a new spirit; for why will you die?" (ibid. 18:31). And they said, of blessed memory, concerning "the death of the dying" - that the wicked in his lifetime is called dead, and yet, "let him return, and live." Further, in another passage there (33:10-12): "son of man, say to the house of Israel, thus you speak, saying: our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we pine away in them; how then shall we live? Say to them, as I live, says the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn, turn from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel? And you, son of man, say to the children of your people, the righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him in the day of his transgression, and as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall thereby in the day that he turns from his wickedness; neither shall the righteous be able to live for his righteousness in the day that he sins" - and the rest of the passage stated there, hear it and know it for yourself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:59: And so all the prophets that stood for Israel stood for them only to turn them back in repentance - and since their words are written before us, it is as though the prophet were alive and standing, teaching us the ways of repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:60: And concerning this aspect of awakening, they said, of blessed memory, in the Pesikta (D'Rav Kahana, section 24), concerning the matter of repentance, "return, O Israel" (Hosea 14:2): a parable of a province troubled by marauding bands, in which there was a certain elder who warned all the people of the province, and whoever heeded him would be saved, and whoever did not heed him, the marauding bands would come upon him and kill him - and therefore the prophet cries out and says, "return, O Israel." And it is taught in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: "the Mikveh of Israel is the LORD" (Jeremiah 17:13) - just as a mikveh purifies the impure, so the Holy One, blessed be He, purifies Israel through repentance - therefore Hosea warns Israel and says to them, "return, O Israel."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:61: And Rashbi, peace be upon him, summed up these six awakenings we have noted concerning repentance, in a brief discourse (Zohar, Parashat Acharei Mot, end of page 57), in these words: Rabbi Shimon said, I am astonished at the people of the world, for they have no eyes to see nor a heart to pay attention, and they do not know, nor do they set their hearts to gaze upon the will of their Master - how do they sleep and not awaken from their sleep, before that day comes that covers them with darkness and complaint, and that Owner of the deposit demands a reckoning from them? And a herald calls over them every day, and their soul testifies against them every day and night, and the Torah raises its voice on every side, proclaiming and saying (Proverbs 1:22), "how long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?" Who is simple, let him turn in here; to him who lacks understanding, she says (ibid. 9:4), "come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine I have mixed" - and there is none who inclines his ear, and none who arouses his heart - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:62: The first three awakenings I explained are included in his words, in saying "and they do not set their hearts to gaze upon the will of their Master" - for His will, blessed be He, is that we repair our souls, which are a portion of Him, and that we repent so as not to need the refining fire of Gehinnom, and likewise that we repair the exile of His Shechinah. And he says, "I am astonished at the people of the world" - at those whose whole intent is on the affairs of this world and not on the affairs of the supernal world - "for they have no eyes to see" - meaning, that eyes and heart were created in them in vain, for the eyes were essentially created so that a person gaze through them at spiritual things, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 8, and the heart to be cleaved to the simple will that is in the Name, blessed be He, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel, page 128b) concerning "whose heart made him willing" - and we shall copy his words concerning prayer, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:63: The fourth awakening, concerning the matter of the days, he says, "how do they sleep and not awaken, before that day comes," and so on. The fifth awakening, from the herald, he says, "and a herald." And the sixth, "the Torah raises its voice on every side" - for in the Torah is written the matter of several promises He promised through the prophets concerning repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:64: And further he added a seventh awakening, which is the soul that testifies against him every day - namely, the thoughts of repentance that come to a person every day, for there is no wicked person of Israel who does not have thoughts of repentance, except that his inclination overpowers him and seduces him afterward; and likewise sometimes the soul is aroused by some bad dream, to awaken him to repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:65: The eighth awakening is that it is fitting to consider how many we find who repented and were accepted. First, Adam, the first man - they said in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 20): on the first day of the week, Adam entered into the upper waters of the Gichon until the water reached his neck, and he fasted seven weeks of days, until his body became like a sieve. Adam said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of all worlds, remove my sin from me and accept my repentance, and let all generations learn that there is repentance, and that You accept the repentance of those who return. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He stretched out His right hand and removed his sin from him and accepted his repentance, as it is said (Psalms 32:5), "I acknowledged my sin to You, and my iniquity I have not hidden," and so on, "You have forgiven the iniquity of my sin, Selah" - "Selah" from this world, and "Selah" from the World to Come - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:66: And so they said in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 18), that the psalm "a song for the Sabbath day" was said by Adam, the first man - for on the eve of Shabbat he was expelled from the Garden of Eden, and Shabbat came and became an advocate for Adam, and so on. And he further says: this verse (Psalms 92:2), "it is good to give thanks to the LORD," was said by Adam, the first man, so that all generations would learn that whoever acknowledges his transgressions and abandons them is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom, as it is said, "it is good to give thanks" - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:67: Further, they said in Bereshit Rabbah (21:6), on "and now, lest he put forth his hand" (Genesis 3:22): Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said, this teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, opened for him an opening of repentance, as it is said, "and now, lest he put forth" - and it is written (Deuteronomy 10:12), "and now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:68: And further, we learn in Bereshit Rabbah (22:13): "and Cain went out from the presence of the LORD" (Genesis 4:16) - to where did he go? Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Huna bar Yitzchak: he went out rejoicing, along the lines of what is said (Exodus 4:14), "and also, behold, he comes forth to meet you," and so on. Adam, the first man, met him and said to him, what became of your judgment? He said to him, I repented and reached a settlement. Adam began to strike his own face and said, such is the power of repentance, and I did not know! Immediately he rose and said, "a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," and so on - to this point, relevant here.
